problems.title: Find the probability if the density function is given
problems.problem:
The mileage $C$ in thousands of kilometers which car owners get with a certain kind of tyres is a random variable having probability density function \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{20}e^{-\frac{x}{20}}, &\text{ if } x > 0;\\ 0, &\text{ if } x \leq 0. \end{cases} \] Find the probabilities that one of these tyres will last
  • at most $10,000$ kilometers;
  • anywhere from $16,000$ to $24,000$ kilometers;
  • at least $30,000$ kilometers.
problems.solution:
The given probability distribution function is \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{20}e^{-\frac{x}{20}}, &\text{ if } x > 0;\\ 0, &\text{ if } x \leq 0. \end{cases} \] Let $X$ denote the millage in thousand kilometers with a certain kind of tyre.
  • We need to find the probability that one of the tyres will last at most $10,000$ kilometers. It will be \begin{align*} P( X \leq 10) & = \int _{-\infty }^{10} f(x) \mathrm{d} x\\ & = \int _0^{10} \frac{1}{20} e^{-\frac{x}{20}} \mathrm{d} x \\[1ex] & = \frac{1}{20} \left[ \dfrac{e^{-\frac{x}{20}}}{-1 / 20} \right]_0^{10} \\[1ex] & = \left[ -e^{-\frac{10}{20}} + e^{\frac{0}{20}} \right] \\[1ex] & = 1 - e^{-\frac{1}{2}} = 0.3935. \end{align*}
  • The probability that one of the tyres will last between $16,000$ to $24,000$ kilometers will be \begin{align*} P(16 \le X \le 24) & = \int_{16}^{24} f(x) \mathrm{d} x \\ & = \frac{1}{20} \int_{16}^{24} e^{-\frac{x}{20}} \mathrm{d} x \\[1ex] & = \frac{1}{20}\left[ \dfrac{e^{-\frac{x}{20}}}{-1 / 20} \right]_{16}^{24} \\[1ex] & = \left[ - e^{-\frac{24}{20}} + e^{-\frac{16}{20}} \right] \\[1ex] & = e^{-\frac{4}{5}} - e^{-\frac{6}{5}} \\ & = 0.1481. \end{align*}
  • Finally, the probability that one of the tyres will last at least $30,000$ kilometers will be \begin{align*} P(X \geq 30) & = \int_{30}^{\infty} f(x)\mathrm{d} x\\ & = \frac{1}{20} \int_{30}^{\infty } e^{-\frac{x}{20}} \mathrm{d} x\\[1ex] & = \frac{1}{20} \left[ \dfrac{e^{-\frac{x}{20}}}{-1 /20} \right]_{30}^{\infty } \\[1ex] & = e^{-\frac{30}{20}} = 0.2231. \end{align*}

problems.title: Use Newton-Raphson method to evaluate $\sqrt{13}$ correct up to $4$ decimal places
problems.problem: Use Newton-Raphson method to evaluate $\sqrt{13}$ correct up to $4$ decimal places.
problems.solution:
e want to find the value of $\sqrt{13}$ by Newton-Raphson's method. For that, take the function $f(x) = x^2 - 13$. Clearly, one of the roots of the equation $f(x) = 0$ is $\sqrt{13}$. We will approximate this using the Newton-Raphson method. We have \[ f(x) = x^2 - 13 \quad \text{and} \quad f'(x) = 2x. \] Thus, the Newton-Raphson iteration scheme will be \begin{align*} x_{n+1} & = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} \\ & = x_n - \frac{x_n^2 - 13}{2 x_n}, \quad n \geq 0. \end{align*} We will start with an initial guess of $x_0 = 1$. Since $f'(1) = 2 \neq 0$, this guess is a valid guess.
  • First iteration: $x_0 = 1$. \[ x_1 = x_0 - \frac{x_0^2 - 13}{2 x_0} = 7. \]
  • Second iteration: $x_1 = 7$. \[ x_2 = x_1 - \frac{x_1^2 - 13}{2 x_1} = 4.4285714. \]
  • Third iteration: $x_2 = 4.4285714$. \[ x_3 = x_2 - \frac{x_2^2 - 13}{2 x_2} = 3.6820276. \]
  • Fourth iteration: $x_3 = 3.6820276$. \[ x_4 = x_3 - \frac{x_3^2 - 13}{2 x_3} = 3.606345. \]
  • Fifth iteration: $x_4 = 3.606345$. \[ x_5 = x_4 - \frac{x_4^2 - 13}{2 x_4} = 3.605551. \]
  • Sixth iteration: $x_5 = 3.605551$. \[ x_6 = x_5 - \frac{x_5^2 - 13}{2 x_5} = 3.605551. \]
Thus, the value $\sqrt{13}$ correct to 4 decimal places is $3.6055$.

problems.title: Percentage of Male and Female Employees
problems.problem: The average salary of male employees in a firm was Rs $520$ and that of a female was Rs $420$. The mean salary of all employees was Rs. $500$. Find the percentage of male and female employees.
problems.solution: Let $n_m$, $n_f$ denote the number of male and female employees in the firm respectively. Further assume that \begin{align*} x_m & = \text{ the average salary of male employees } \\ x_f & = \text{ the average salary of female employees } \\ x & = \text{ average salary of all the employees } . \end{align*} According to the problem, \begin{align*} x_m = 520 \quad x_w = 420 \quad \text{ and } \quad x = 500. \end{align*} We have \begin{align*} x = \frac{n_m x_m + n_f x_f}{n_m + n_f} & \implies 500 = \frac{520 n_m + 420 n_f}{n_m + n_f}\\ & \implies 500(n_m + n_f) = 520 n_m + 420 n_f\\ & \implies 20 n_m - 80 n_f = 0 \\ & \implies \frac{n_m}{n_f} = \frac{4}{1}. \end{align*} Therefore, the percentage of male employees in the firm will be \[ \frac{4}{4 + 1} \times 100 = 80\% \] and the percentage of male employees in the firm will be \[ \frac{1}{4 + 1} \times 100 = 20\%. \]

problems.title: Find The Second Derivative of an Implicit Function
problems.problem: Find $\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} $ if $x^4 + y^4 = 16$.
problems.solution: The given equation is \begin{equation}\label{eq:11Jan2025-1} x^4 + y^4 = 1. \end{equation} Differentiating equation \eqref{eq:11Jan2025-1}, we get \begin{equation}\label{eq:11Jan2025-2} 4x^3 + 4 y^3 \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0. \end{equation} Again differentiating the equation \eqref{eq:11Jan2025-2} with respect to $x$, we get \begin{equation}\label{eq:11Jan2025-3} 12x^2 + 12 y^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} + 4y^3 \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = 0 . \end{equation} Using equation \eqref{eq:11Jan2025-2}, we have \begin{equation}\label{eq:11Jan2025-4} \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = - \frac{x^3}{y^3}. \end{equation} Substituting the above into equation \eqref{eq:11Jan2025-3}, we get \begin{align*} & 12x^2 + 12y^2 \left[ -\frac{x^3}{y^3} \right] + 4y^3 \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = 0 \\ \implies & 4y^3 \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = -12x^2 + \frac{12x^3}{y} \\ \implies & \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} = \frac{3x^3}{y^4} - \frac{3x^2}{y^3} = \frac{3x^3 - 3x^2 y}{y^4}. \end{align*} Thus, \[ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{ \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 y}{\mathrm{d} x^2} = \frac{3x^3 - 3x^2 y}{y^4} }} \]

problems.title: Probability and Set Operations
problems.problem:
Let $A$ and $B$ be two events such that
\[
    P(A) = \frac{3}{4} \text{ and } P(B) = \frac{5}{8}.
\]
Show that
\[
    P(A  \cup B) \geq \frac{3}{4} \text{ and } \frac{3}{8} \leq P(A  \cap B) \leq \frac{5}{8}.
\]
problems.solution:
We recall that for given set $A$ and $B$ if $A \subseteq B$, then the corresponding probabilities are $P(A) \leq P(B)$. So, we have \begin{align*} A \subseteq A \cup B & \implies P(A) \leq P(A \cup B) \\ & \implies \frac{3}{4} \leq P(A \cup B). \end{align*} This proves that \[ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{ P(A \cup B) \geq \frac{3}{4} }} \]
We also recall that for any two events $A$ and $B$, we have \[ P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B). \] Using this, we get \[ P(A \cup B) = \frac{3}{4} + \frac{5}{8} - P(A \cap B). \] Since $P(A \cup B) \leq 1$, we have \[ \frac{3}{4} + \frac{5}{8} - P(A \cap B) \leq 1 \implies P(A \cap B) \geq \frac{3}{8}. \] Also, since $A \cap B \subseteq B$, we have $P(A \cap B) \leq P(B)$, we have \[ P(A \cap B) \leq \frac{5}{8}. \] Thus, \[ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{ \frac{3}{8} \leq P(A \cap B) \leq \frac{5}{8} }} \]

problems.title: Infinite Series Sum (arithmetic-geometric series)
problems.problem:
Find the value of
\[
    \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^n.
\]
problems.solution:
Note that the given sequence is an arithmetic-geometric series. Let \[ S = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^n. \] First of all, we will show that the given series is convergent. For that, we will use the ratio test. Consider the general term of the series: \[ a_n = n \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^n. \] We need to find the limit \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|. \] We have \begin{align*} \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} & = \frac{(n+1) \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^{n+1}}{n \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^n} \\ & = \frac{n+1}{2n}. \end{align*} Taking the limit as \( n \) approaches infinity, we get \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n+1}{2n} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1 + \frac{1}{n}}{2} = \frac{1}{2}. \] Since the limit is less than $1$, the ratio test confirms that the series is convergent.
Now we assume that \[ S = 0 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^0 + 1 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^1 + 2 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^2 + 3 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^3 + \cdots \] Multiplying both sides by $\frac{1}{2}$, we get \[ \frac{S}{2} = 0 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^1 + 1 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^2 + 2 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^3 + 3 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^4 + \cdots \] Subtracting the above equation from $S$, we get \begin{align*} S - \frac{S}{2} & = \left( 1 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^1 + 2 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^2 + 3 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^3 + \cdots \right) \\ & \quad - \left( 0 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^1 + 1 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^2 + 2 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^3 + \cdots \right) \\[1ex] \implies \frac{S}{2} & = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2^2} + \frac{1}{2^3} + \cdots \\[1ex] \implies S & = 2 \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^n = 2 \left( \frac{\frac{1}{2}}{1-\frac{1}{2}} \right) = 2. \end{align*} Thus, \[ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^n = 2 }} \]

problems.title: A Problem on Mean Value Theorem
problems.problem: A function $f(x) = 1 - x^2 + x^3$ is defined in the closed interval $[-1,1]$. The value of $\xi \in (-1,1)$ for which the mean value theorem is satisfied, is
problems.solution:
According to the mean value theorem, if a function $f(x)$ is continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$, then there exists at least one point $\xi \in (a, b)$ such that \[ f'(\xi) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}. \] Here, $f(x) = 1 - x^2 + x^3$, which is a polynomial and hence is continuous and differentiable on $[-1, 1]$. We need to find $\xi \in (-1, 1)$ such that \[ f'(\xi) = \frac{f(1) - f(-1)}{1 - (-1)}. \] First, we calculate $f(1)$ and $f(-1)$: \begin{align*} & f(1) = 1 - 1^2 + 1^3 = 1 \\ & f(-1) = 1 - (-1)^2 + (-1)^3 = -1. \end{align*} Thus, \[ \frac{f(1) - f(-1)}{1 - (-1)} = \frac{1 - (-1)}{2} = \frac{2}{2} = 1. \]
Next, we find $f'(x)$: \[ f'(x) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x} (1 - x^2 + x^3) = -2x + 3x^2. \] We need to solve for $\xi$ such that \begin{align*} f'(\xi ) = 1 & \implies -2\xi + 3\xi^2 = 1 \\ & \implies 3\xi^2 - 2\xi - 1 = 0 \\ & \implies (3\xi +1)(\xi - 1) = 0. \end{align*} Thus, \[ \xi = 1 \quad \text{or} \quad \xi = -\frac{1}{3}. \] Since $\xi$ must be in the interval $(-1, 1)$, we have \[ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{\xi = -\frac{1}{3}}} \]

problems.title: Find the value of the infinite sum $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\pi ^n}{n!}$
problems.problem: Find the value of the infinite sum $\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\pi ^n}{n!}$.
problems.solution: We recall that the Taylor's series expansion for $e^x$ is given by \[ e^x = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n!}. \] Setting $x = \pi $, we get \[ e^\pi = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\pi ^n}{n!}. \] Thus, the value of the infinite sum is \[ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{ \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!} = e }} \]

problems.title: An Integral Similar to Gaussian Integral
problems.problem:
Find the value of the integral
\[
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi } } \int _0^{\infty} e^{-x^2 / 8} \mathrm{d} x .
\]
problems.solution:
At first we recall the Gaussian integral \[ \int _{-\infty }^{\infty} e^{-x^2} \mathrm{d} x = \sqrt{\pi }. \] We can compute the Gaussian integral by using the double integral as follows: \[ \left( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} \mathrm{d}x \right)^2 = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2 - y^2} \mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y. \] Switching to polar coordinates, where \( x = r \cos \theta \) and \( y = r \sin \theta \), we get \[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2 - y^2} \mathrm{d}x \mathrm{d}y = \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-r^2} r \mathrm{d}r \mathrm{d}\theta. \] The integral simplifies to \[ \int_{0}^{2\pi} \mathrm{d}\theta \int_{0}^{\infty} r e^{-r^2} \mathrm{d}r. \] Evaluating the inner integral, we use the substitution \( u = r^2 \), \( \mathrm{d}u = 2r \mathrm{d}r \), giving \[ \int_{0}^{\infty} r e^{-r^2} \mathrm{d}r = \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-u} \mathrm{d}u = \frac{1}{2}. \] Thus, the double integral becomes \[ \int_{0}^{2\pi} \mathrm{d}\theta \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \pi. \] Therefore, \[ \left( \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} \mathrm{d}x \right)^2 = \pi \implies \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} \mathrm{d}x = \sqrt{\pi}. \] This also implies (as $e^{-x^2} $ is an even function ) \[ \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} \mathrm{d}x = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}. \]
Now, we need to compute the given integral. Note that \[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-x^2 / 8} \mathrm{d}x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(x/\sqrt{8})^2} \mathrm{d}x. \] Let \( u = \frac{x}{\sqrt{8}} \), then \( \mathrm{d}x = \sqrt{8} \mathrm{d}u \), and the integral becomes \begin{align*} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-u^2} \sqrt{8} \mathrm{d}u & = \frac{\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-u^2} \mathrm{d}u \\[1ex] & = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi } } \left( \frac{\sqrt{\pi } }{2} \right) \\[1ex] & = 1. \end{align*} Thus, \[ \textcolor{blue}{ \boxed{ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi } } \int _0^{\infty} e^{-x^2 / 8} \mathrm{d} x = 1. } } \]

problems.title: Solving Differential Equation by Picard's Iteration
problems.problem:
Apply Picard's iteration to solve the following initial value problem up to third approximation.
\[
    \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2y - 2x^2 - 3, \quad y(0) = 2.
\]
problems.hint:
1. The Picard's iteration for the initial value problem \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = f(x, y), \quad y(x_0) = y_0 \] is given by the iterative formula \[ y_{n+1}(x) = y_0 + \int_{x_0}^{x} f(t, y_n(t)) \, \mathrm{d}t. \]
  2. The iteration formula will be \[ y_{n+1}(x) = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 2y_n(t) - 2t^2 - 3 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t. \]
problems.solution:
We recall that the Picard's iteration for the initial value problem \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = f(x, y), \quad y(x_0) = y_0 \] is given by the iterative formula \[ y_{n+1}(x) = y_0 + \int_{x_0}^{x} f(t, y_n(t)) \, \mathrm{d}t. \] For the given problem, we have \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 2y - 2x^2 - 3, \quad y(0) = 2. \] Thus, the iterative formula becomes \[ y_{n+1}(x) = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 2y_n(t) - 2t^2 - 3 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t. \]
Starting with the initial approximation \( y_0(x) = 2 \), we compute the next approximations as follows:

First Approximation: $y_0(x) = 2$. \begin{align*} y_{1}(x) & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 2y_0(t) - 2t^2 - 3 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t \\ & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 2 \cdot 2 - 2t^2 - 3 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t \\ & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 4 - 2t^2 - 3 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t \\ & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 1 - 2t^2 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t\\ & = 2 + \left[ t - \frac{2t^3}{3} \right]_{0}^{x} \\ & = 2 + \left( x - \frac{2x^3}{3} \right) \\ & = 2 + x - \frac{2x^3}{3}. \end{align*}
Second Approximation: $y_1(x) = 2 + x - \frac{2x^3}{3}.$ \begin{align*} y_2(x) & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 2 \left( 2 + t - \frac{2t^3}{3} \right) - 2t^2 - 3 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t \\ & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 4 + 2t - \frac{4t^3}{3} - 2t^2 - 3 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t \\ & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 1 + 2t - 2t^2 - \frac{4t^3}{3} \right) \, \mathrm{d}t\\ & = 2 + \left[ t + t^2 - \frac{2t^3}{3} - \frac{t^4}{3} \right]_{0}^{x}\\ & = 2 + x + x^2 - \frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{3}. \end{align*}
Third Approximation: $y_2(x) = 2 + x + x^2 - \frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{3}.$ \begin{align*} y_3(x) & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 2 \left( 2 + t + t^2 - \frac{2t^3}{3} - \frac{t^4}{3} \right) - 2t^2 - 3 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t \\ & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 4 + 2t + 2t^2 - \frac{4t^3}{3} - \frac{2t^4}{3} - 2t^2 - 3 \right) \, \mathrm{d}t \\ & = 2 + \int_{0}^{x} \left( 1 + 2t - \frac{4t^3}{3} - \frac{2t^4}{3} \right) \, \mathrm{d}t \\ & = 2 + \left[ t + t^2 - \frac{t^4}{3} - \frac{2t^5}{15} \right]_{0}^{x} \\ & = 2 + x + x^2 - \frac{x^4}{3} - \frac{2x^5}{15}. \end{align*} Thus, the third approximation is \[ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{ y_3(x) = 2 + x + x^2 - \frac{x^4}{3} - \frac{2x^5}{15} }} \]

problems.title: Calculus - Stationary point of the curve $y = x^2 - 2x - 24\sqrt{x}$
problems.problem:
A curve $C$ has equation \[ y = x^2 - 2x - 24 \sqrt{x}, \quad x > 0. \]
  1. Find $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} $.
  2. Find the second derivative $\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}$.
  3. Verify that $C$ has a stationary point when $x = 4$.
  4. Determine the nature of the stationary point at $x = 4$.
problems.hint:
1. The stationary points of a curve are the points where the first derivative is zero.
  2. The nature of the stationary point can be determined by the second derivative. If the second derivative is positive, the stationary point is a local minimum. If the second derivative is negative, the stationary point is a local maximum.
problems.solution:
The given curve $C$ is defined by the equation \begin{equation}\label{eq:01Mar2025-1} y = x^2 - 2x - 24 \sqrt{x}. \end{equation}
  1. Differentiating equation \eqref{eq:01Mar2025-1} with respect to $x$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} & = 2x - 2 - 12 \left( x \right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ & = 2x - 2 - \frac{12}{\sqrt{x}}. \end{align*}
  2. For the second derivative, $\frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}$, differentiate the expression for $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$ with respect to $x$ to get \begin{align*} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2} & = 2 + 6 x^{-\frac{3}{2}} = 2 + \frac{6}{x^{3/2}}. \end{align*}
  3. To verify that $C$ has a stationary point when $x = 4$, we need to check if $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 0$ at $x = 4$. Substituting $x = 4$ into $\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}$, we get \begin{align*} \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}\bigg|_{x=4} & = 2(4) - 2 - \frac{12}{\sqrt{4}} \\ & = 8 - 2 - 6 \\ & = 0. \end{align*} This confirms that there is a stationary point at $x = 4$.
  4. Next, we check the second derivative at the stationary point to determine its nature: \begin{align*} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}\bigg|_{x=4} & = 2 + 6(4)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \\ & = 2 + 6 \cdot \frac{1}{8} = \frac{11}{4} > 0. \end{align*} This indicates that the stationary point at $x = 4$ is a local minimum.

problems.title: Solving the Exponential Equation \((x^2 - 9x + 19)^{(x^2 - 15x + 56)} = 1\) for Integer Solutions
problems.problem:
Solve
\[
    \left( x^2 - 9x + 19 \right) ^{\left( x^2 - 15x + 56 \right) } = 1
\]
and find all possible integer values of $x$.
problems.hint:
Note that $x^y = 1$ holds in integers if and only if either of the following holds:
  1. $x = 1$ and $y \in \mathbb{Z} $;
  2. $x \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{ 0 \} $ and $y = 0$;
  3. $x = - 1$ and $y$ is even.
problems.solution:
The given equation is \begin{equation}\label{eq:08Mar2025-1} \left( x^2 - 9x + 19 \right) ^{\left( x^2 - 15x + 56 \right) } = 1. \end{equation} We note that $x^y = 1$ holds in integers if and only if either of the following holds:
  1. $x = 1$ and $y \in \mathbb{Z} $;
  2. $x \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{ 0 \} $ and $y = 0$;
  3. $x = - 1$ and $y$ is even.
We will take these three cases into consideration.

Case 1: Let \( x^2 - 9x + 19 = 1 \) and $x^2 - 15x + 56 \in \mathbb{Z} $. Thus, \begin{align*} x^2 - 9x + 19 = 1 & \implies x^2 - 9x + 18 = 0 \\ & \implies (x-3)(x-6) = 0 \\ & \implies x = 3 \text{ or } x = 6. \end{align*}
Case 2: Let \( x^2 - 9x + 19 \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{ 0 \} \) and $x^2 - 15x + 56 = 0$. Thus, \begin{align*} x^2 - 15x + 56 = 0 & \implies (x - 7) (x - 8) = 0 \\ & \implies x = 7 \text{ or } x = 8. \end{align*} Note that for $x = 7$ or $x = 8$, $x^2 - 9x + 19 \neq 0$.
Case 3: Let \( x^2 - 9x + 19 = -1 \) and \( x^2 - 15x + 56 \) is even. Then we have \begin{align*} x^2 - 9x + 19 = -1 & \implies x^2 - 9x + 20 = 0 \\ & \implies (x - 4)(x - 5) = 0 \\ & \implies x = 4 \text{ or } x = 5. \end{align*} Putting these values in $x^2 - 15x + 56 $, we get $12$ and $6$. Thus both values are possible. Therefore, the solution of the equation \eqref{eq:08Mar2025-1} in $\mathbb{Z} $ will be $3,4,5,6,7,8$.

problems.title: Determine the value of a and find P(X ≤ 1.5) for a given probability density function
problems.problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with probability density function given by
\[
    f(x) =
    \begin{cases}
        ax, & 0 \leq x \leq 1 ;\\
        a, & 1 \leq x \leq 2 ;\\
        -ax + 3a, & 2 \leq x \leq 3 ;\\
        0, & \text{ otherwise } \\
    \end{cases}
\]
Determine the value of $a$ and find $P(X \leq 1.5)$.
problems.hint:
1. The total probability is $1$, that is \[ P(X < \infty) = 1 \implies \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\ \mathrm{d}x = 1\]
  2. $P(X < a) = \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^a f(x)\ \mathrm{d}x$.
problems.solution:
We know that the total probability of any event is $1$, so \begin{align*} & \int_{-\infty }^ {\infty } f(x) \mathrm{d} x = 1 \\[2ex] \implies & \int_{-\infty } ^ 0 0\ \mathrm{d} x + \int _0 ^ 1 ax\ \mathrm{d} x + \int_1 ^2 a\ \mathrm{d} x \\[1ex] & \kern 1cm + \int_2 ^3 (-ax + 3a)\ \mathrm{d} x + \int_3 ^{\infty } 0 \ \mathrm{d} x = 1 \\[2ex] \implies & \left[ \frac{ax^2}{2} \right]_0^1 + \left[ ax \right] _1^2 + \left[ \frac{-ax^2}{2} + 3ax \right]_2^3 = 1\\[2ex] \implies & \left[ \frac{a}{2} - 0 \right] + (2a - a) + \left[ -\frac{9a}{2} + 9a + 2a - 6a \right] = 1 \\[2ex] \implies & 2a = 1 \implies a = \frac{1}{2}. \end{align*} Thus, \[ \textcolor{blue}{ \boxed{ a = \frac{1}{2} } } \]
Now we need to find the probability of the even when $X \leq 1.5$. This will be \begin{align*} P(X \leq 1.5) & = \int_{-\infty }^{1.5} f(x)\ \mathrm{d} x \\ & = \int_0^1 ax\ \mathrm{d} x + \int_1^{1.5} a\ \mathrm{d} x \\ & = a\left[ \frac{x^2}{2} \right]_0^1 + a (0.5) \\ & = \frac{a}{2} + \frac{a}{2} = a = \frac{1}{2}. \end{align*} Thus, \[ \textcolor{blue}{\boxed{ P(X \leq 1.5) = 1.5 }} \]

problems.title: Find Potential Function for the Irrotational Flow $\mathbf{v} = (y + z)\mathbf{i} + (z + x) \mathbf{j} + (x + y)\mathbf{k}$
problems.problem: A fluid motion is given by $\mathbf{v} = (y + z)\mathbf{i} + (z + x) \mathbf{j} + (x + y)\mathbf{k} $. Show that the motion is irrotational and hence find the scalar potential.
problems.hint:
1. A vector field in $\mathbb{R} ^3$ is irrotational if its curl is zero.
  2. To find the potential function $\phi$, solve the system \[ (y + z)\mathbf{i} + (z + x) \mathbf{j} + (x + y)\mathbf{k} = \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial y} \mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial z} \mathbf{k}. \]
problems.solution:
We recall that a vector field in $\mathbb{R} ^3$ is irrotational if its curl is zero. We also recall that for a vector field $\mathbf{v} = v_1 \mathbf{i} + v_2 \mathbf{j} + v_3 \mathbf{k}$, the curl is given by \[ \mathrm{curl}(\mathbf{v} ) = \nabla \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x} & \frac{\partial }{\partial y} & \frac{\partial }{\partial z} \\ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{vmatrix}. \] Thus the curl of the given vector field will be \begin{align*} \nabla \times \mathbf{v} & = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x} & \frac{\partial }{\partial y} & \frac{\partial }{\partial z} \\ (y+z) & (z+x) & (x + y) \\ \end{vmatrix} \\ & = \left[ 1 - 1 \right] \mathbf{i} - \left[ 1 - 1 \right] \mathbf{j} + \left[ 1 -1 \right] \mathbf{k} = \mathbf{0} . \end{align*} Thus, the given vector filed id irrotational.
Since $\mathbf{v} $ is irrotational, we can find a scalar function (potential function) $\phi $ such that $\mathbf{v} = \mathrm{grad} (\phi)$. Thus we have \begin{equation}\label{eq:22Mar2025-1} (y + z)\mathbf{i} + (z + x) \mathbf{j} + (x + y)\mathbf{k} = \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial y} \mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial z} \mathbf{k}. \end{equation} This gives a system of equations \begin{align*} \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x} = ( y + z) \implies \phi (x,y,z) & = \int (y +z) \ \mathrm{d} x + f(y,z) \\ & = x(y+z) + f(y,z), \end{align*} where $f(y,z)$ is a function of only $y$ and $z$.
Now differentiating $\phi $ with respect $y$ and from the equation \eqref{eq:22Mar2025-1}, \begin{align*} \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial y} = (z + x) & \implies x + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = z + x \\ & \implies \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = z \\ & \implies f(y,z) = yz + g(z), \end{align*} where $g$ is the function of $z$ only. Thus, $\phi (x,y,z) = x(y+z) + yz + g(z)$. Finally, \begin{align*} \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial z} = (x + y) & \implies x + y + g'(z) = x + y \\ & \implies g'(z) = 0\\ & \implies g(z) = c \text{ (constant) }. \end{align*} Therefore, \[ \textcolor{blue}{ \boxed{ \phi (x,y,z) = xy + yz + zx + c } } \]

problems.title: NBHM 2019 Solution - Find the number of integer solutions to the equation x² + 16 = y²
problems.problem: The number of solutions $(x,y) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z} $ of the equation $x^2 + 16 = y^2$ is ___________________.
problems.hint:
1. Rearrange the equation as $x^2 - y^2 = -16$, which further simplifies to $(x-y)(x+y) = -16$.
  2. Now consider the factors of $-16$. Since $x-y$ and $x+y$ are integers, both $x$ and $y$ must be even or both must be odd.
problems.solution: The given equation is $x^2 + 16 = y^2$, which can be rearranged as \[ x^2 - y^2 = -16 \implies (x-y)(x+y) = -16. \] As we know that both $x$ and $y$ are integers and hence $x-y$ and $x+y$ are also integers. Let $-16 = a \times b$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers, then the possible values of $a$ and $b$ are \begin{align*} (\pm 1, \mp 16), (\pm 16, \mp 1), (\pm 2, \mp 8), (\pm 8, \mp 2), (\pm 4, \mp 4). \end{align*} If $x - y = a$ and $x + y = b$, then \[ x = \frac{a+b}{2} \quad \text{ and } \quad y = \frac{b-a}{2}. \] As $x, y \in \mathbb{Z} $, so $a$ and $b$ must have the same parity. Thus, we have the following pairs of $(a,b)$: \[ (\pm 2, \mp 8), (\pm 8, \mp 2), (\pm 4, \mp 4). \] Hence, the number of integral solutions to the equation $x^2 + 16 = y^2$ is $6$.

problems.title: Given a quartic equation with two positive and two negative roots such that αβ = γδ = 4, find the constants k and m, evaluate (α+β)(γ+δ), and determine a quadratic with roots α+β and γ+δ
problems.problem:
The equation $x^4 - 6x^3 - 73 x^2 + kx + m = 0$ has two positive roots $\alpha ,\beta $ and two negative roots $\gamma , \delta $. It is given that $\alpha \beta = \gamma \delta = 4$.
  1. Find the values of the constant $k$ and $m$.
  2. Show that $(\alpha +\beta )(\gamma + \delta ) = -81$.
  3. Find the quadratic equation which has roots $\alpha + \beta $ and $\gamma + \delta $.
problems.hint: 1. For the equation, we have \begin{gather*} \alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = 6, \\ \alpha \beta + \alpha \gamma + \alpha \delta + \beta \gamma + \beta \delta + \gamma \delta = -73,\\ \alpha \beta (\gamma +\delta ) + \gamma \delta(\alpha +\beta ) = -k,\\ \alpha \beta \gamma \delta = m. \end{gather*}
problems.solution:
The given equation is \begin{equation}\label{eq:05Apr2025-1} x^4 - 6x^3 - 73 x^2 + kx + m = 0. \end{equation} Since $\alpha ,\beta ,\gamma ,\delta $ are roots of the equation \eqref{eq:05Apr2025-1}, we have \begin{gather*} \alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = 6, \\ \alpha \beta + \alpha \gamma + \alpha \delta + \beta \gamma + \beta \delta + \gamma \delta = -73,\\ \alpha \beta (\gamma +\delta ) + \gamma \delta(\alpha +\beta ) = -k,\\ \alpha \beta \gamma \delta = m. \end{gather*}
  1. Since $\alpha \beta = 4 = \gamma \delta $, so \begin{align*} \alpha \beta \gamma \delta = 16 \implies m = 16. \end{align*} Now we have \begin{align*} & \alpha \beta (\gamma +\delta ) + \gamma \delta(\alpha +\beta ) = - k \\ \implies & 4(\gamma +\delta ) + 4(\alpha +\beta ) = -k \\ \implies & 4\left( \alpha +\beta +\gamma +\delta \right) = -k \\ \implies & k = -24. \end{align*}
  2. We have \begin{align*} & (\alpha + \beta )(\gamma + \delta ) + \alpha \beta + \gamma \delta = -73 \\ \implies & (\alpha + \beta)(\gamma + \delta) + 8 = -73 \\ \implies & (\alpha + \beta)(\gamma + \delta) = -81 \end{align*}
  3. The quadratic equation with roots $\alpha + \beta $ and $\gamma + \delta $ is given by \[ x^2 - (\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta )x + (\alpha + \beta)(\gamma + \delta ) = 0. \] Since $\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = 6 $ and $(\alpha + \beta)(\gamma + \delta) = -81$. Thus the quadratic equation is \[ x^2 - 6x - 81 = 0. \]

problems.title: Biased Dice with Inverse Probability Weights
problems.problem:
A biased four-sided dice with faces numbered $1, 2, 3$ and $4$ is rolled. The number on the bottommost face is modelled as a random variable $X$. Given that \[ P(X = x) = \frac{k}{x}. \]
  1. Find the value of $k$.
  2. Give the probability distribution of $X$ in table form.
  3. Find the probability that \[ \text{(i) } X > 2, \quad \text{(ii) } 1 < X < 4 \quad \text{(iii) } X > 4. \]
problems.hint: The sum of probabilities is $1$, that is, \[ \sum_{x \in \{ 1,2,3,4 \} } P(X = x) = 1 \]
problems.solution:
Given that \[ P(X = x) = \frac{k}{x}. \]
  1. Since \begin{align*} \sum_{x \in \{ 1,2,3,4 \} } P(X = x) = 1 & \implies \sum_{x \in \{ 1,2,3,4 \} } \frac{k}{x} = 1 \\ & \implies k + \frac{k}{2} + \frac{k}{3} + \frac{k}{4} = 1 \\ & \implies k = \frac{12}{25}. \end{align*}
  2. Since, $k = \frac{12}{25}$, the probability distribution table is given by \[\def\arraystretch{2} \begin{array}{|ccccc|} \hline X & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X = x) & \dfrac{12}{25} & \dfrac{6}{25} & \dfrac{4}{25} & \dfrac{3}{25} \\[1ex]\hline \end{array} \]
  3. From the above table, we can find the following probabilities. \begin{align*} P(X > 2) & = \frac{4}{25} + \frac{3}{25} = \frac{7}{25}. \\ P(1 < X < 4) & = \frac{6}{25} + \frac{4}{25} = \frac{10}{25} = \frac{2}{5}. \\ P(X > 4) & = 0. \end{align*}

problems.title: Calculus - Find the speed, acceleration and time when particle is at rest
problems.problem:
A particle $P$ is moving on the $x$-axis. At time $t$ seconds, the displacement $x$ meters from $O$ is given by $x = t^4 - 32t + 12$. Find
  1. the speed of $P$ when $t = 3$,
  2. the value of $t$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest,
  3. the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$ when $t = 1.5$.
problems.hint: • The speed $v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} $ and the acceleration is $\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x}{\mathrm{d}t^2} $
problems.solution:
The displacement of the particle is given by the equation \begin{equation}\label{eq:26Apr2025-1} x(t) = t^4 - 32t + 12. \end{equation}
  1. We need to find the speed of $P$ at $t = 3$. At any instance, the speed is given by the derivative. Thus, \begin{align*} v = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} \right|_{t = 3} = (4t^3 - 32)\big|_{t= 3} = 76. \end{align*} Thus, the speed of the particle $P$ at $t=3$ is $76 \mathrm{ms}^{-1} $.
  2. When the body will be at rest, then the velocity will be zero, that is, $v = 0$, Thus, \begin{align*} v = 0 & \implies \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0 \implies 4t^3 - 32 = 0 \\ & \implies t^3 = \frac{32}{4} \implies t = 2. \end{align*}
  3. The acceleration of the particle is the rate of change of the velocity, that is \begin{align*} a = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = 12t^2. \end{align*} Thus, the acceleration at $t = 1.5$ will be \[ a = 12 \times 1.5^2 = 27 \mathrm{ms}^{-2}. \]

problems.title: Calculus - Find the volume of the solid generated by rotating the region bounded by y = 9 - x^2 about the x-axis
problems.problem: The region $R$ which is bounded by the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis and the curve $y = 9- x^2$. The region is rotated through $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Find the volume of the solid generated.
problems.hint: • The volume is given by \[ V = \pi \int_0^3 (9-x^2)^2 \mathrm{d} x \]
problems.solution:
Note that the region $R$ will intersect the $x$-axis when \[ 9 - x^2 = 0 \implies x= \pm 3. \]
The volume of the solid will be given by \begin{align*} V = \pi \int_0^3(9 - x^2)^2 \mathrm{d} x & = \pi \int _0^3 \left( x^4 - 18x^2 + 81 \right) \mathrm{d} x \\ & = \pi \left[ \frac{x^5}{5} - \frac{18x^3}{3} + 81x\right] _0^3 \\ & = \pi \left[ \frac{243}{5} - 162 + 243 \right] \\ & = \frac{648\pi }{5}. \end{align*}

problems.title: Statistics - Test whether X and Y are independent
problems.problem:
Joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ is given by 
    \[
        f(x,y) = 4xy e^{-(x^2 + y^2)}; \quad  x\geq 0,\ y\geq 0.
    \]
    Test whether $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
problems.hint: • The random variables $X$ and $Y$ will be independent if \[ f(x,y) = f_1(x) \cdot f_2(y), \] where $f_1(x)$ is the marginal density of $X$.
problems.solution: The joint probability distribution function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ are given as \[ f(x,y) = 4xy e^{-(x^2 + y^2)}; \quad x\geq 0,\ y\geq 0. \] Marginal density of $X$ is given by \begin{align*} f_1(x) & = \int _0^{\infty} f(x,y) \mathrm{d} y \\ & = \int _0^{\infty} 4xy e^{-(x^2 + y^2)}\mathrm{d} y \\ & = 4xe^{-x^2} \int_0^{\infty} y e^{-y^2} \mathrm{d} y \\ & = 4xe^{-x^2} \int_0^{\infty} e^{-t} \frac{\mathrm{d} t}{2} \qquad (\text{put }t = -y^2) \\ & = 2xe^{-x^2} \left[- e^{-t} \right]_0^{\infty} \\ & = 2xe^{-x^2}, \quad x\geq 0. \end{align*} Similarly, the marginal density of $Y$ is given by \[ f_2(y) = 2ye^{-y^2}, \quad y\geq 0. \] Since \[ f(x,y) = f_1(x) \cdot f_2(y), \] the random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

problems.title: Herstein: 1.1.2 - Set Theory - Verify the properties of the operation * defined on S
problems.problem:
Let $S$ be the set of all integers $0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots.$ For $a,b \in S$ define $*$ by $a * b = a - b$. Verify the following:
  1. $a * b \neq b * a$ unless $a = b$.
  2. $(a * b) * c \neq a * (b * c)$ in general. Under what conditions on $a,b, c$ is $(a * b) * c = a * (b * c)$?
  3. The integer $0$ has the property that $a * 0 = a$ for every $a \in S$.
  4. For $a \in S$, $a * a = 0$.
problems.hint: • Note that $1 * 2 = -1 \neq 2 * 1 = 1$.
problems.solution:
1. Take $a = 1$ and $b = 2$, then \[ 1 * 2 = 1 - 2 = -1 \text{ and } 2 * 1 = 2 - 1 = 1. \] Thus, $a * b \neq b * a$.
  2. For $a = 1$, $b = 2$ and $c = 3$, note that \begin{align*} (a * b) * c & = (1 * 2) * 3 = (1 - 2) - 3 = -4 \\ a * (b * c) & = 1 * (2 * 3) = 1 - (2 - 3) = 2. \end{align*} Thus, $(a * b) * c \neq a * (b * c)$.
  3. For any $a \in S$, \[ a * 0 = a - 0 = a. \]
  4. Note that for any $a \in S$, \[ a * a = a - a = 0. \]

problems.title: Herstein: 1.1.3 - Set Theory - Verify the properties of the operation * defined on S
problems.problem:
Let $S$ consists of two objects $\square$ and $\triangle$. We define the operation $*$ on $S$ by subjecting $\square$ and $\triangle$ the following conditions:
  1. $\square * \triangle = \triangle = \triangle * \square$.
  2. $\square * \square = \square$.
  3. $\triangle * \triangle = \square$.
Verify by explicit calculation that if $a,b,c$ are any elements of $S$ (i.e., $a,b,\text{ and } c$ can be any of $\square$ or $\triangle$), then
  1. $a * b \in S$.
  2. $(a * b) * c = a * (b * c)$.
  3. $a * b = b * a$.
  4. There is a particular element $a \in S$ such that $a * b = b * a = b$ for all $b \in S$.
  5. Given $b \in S$, then $b * b = a$, where $a$ is the particular element in part (iv).
problems.hint: • It's helpful to create a table to visualize the operation $*$ on the elements of $S$. Then, check each property by substituting the elements of $S$ into the operation and verifying the results.
problems.solution:
Note that the following table summarizes the operation $*$ on the elements of $S$: \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{c|c|c} $*$ & $\square$ & $\triangle$ \\ \hline $\square$ & $\square$ & $\triangle$ \\ $\triangle$ & $\triangle$ & $\square$ \\ \end{tabular} \end{center}
  1. We can verify that $a * b \in S$ for all $a, b \in S$ by checking all possible combinations: \begin{align*} \square * \square & = \square \in S, \\ \square * \triangle & = \triangle \in S, \\ \triangle * \square & = \triangle \in S, \\ \triangle * \triangle & = \square \in S. \end{align*} Thus, $a * b \in S$ for all $a, b \in S$.
  2. We can verify that $(a * b) * c = a * (b * c)$ for all $a, b, c \in S$ by checking all possible combinations: \begin{align*} (\square * \square) * \square & = \square * \square = \square = \square * (\square * \square), \\ (\square * \square) * \triangle & = \square * \triangle = \triangle = \square * (\square * \triangle), \\ (\square * \triangle) * \square & = \triangle * \square = \triangle = \square * (\triangle * \square), \\ (\square * \triangle) * \triangle & = \triangle * \triangle = \square = \square * (\triangle * \triangle), \\ (\triangle * \square) * \square & = \triangle * \square = \triangle = \triangle * (\square * \square), \\ (\triangle * \square) * \triangle & = \triangle * \triangle = \square = \triangle * (\square * \triangle), \\ (\triangle * \triangle) * \square & = \square * \square = \square = \triangle * (\triangle * \square), \\ (\triangle * \triangle) * \triangle & = \square * \triangle = \triangle = \triangle * (\triangle * \triangle). \end{align*} Thus, $(a * b) * c = a * (b * c)$ for all $a, b, c \in S$.
  3. From the first part we can see that $a * b = b * a$ for all $a, b \in S$ as \[ \square * \triangle = \triangle = \triangle * \square. \]
  4. The particular element $a \in S$ such that $a * b = b * a = b$ for all $b \in S$ is $\square$. This also follows from the first part.
  5. In the previous part, we have the particular element $\square$ such that for any $b \in S$, we have $b * \square = \square * b = b$. \begin{align*} b = \square \implies b * b = \square * \square = \square, \\ b = \triangle \implies b * b = \triangle * \triangle = \square. \end{align*}

problems.title: Problem of the Day
problems.problem: Prove that $n(n^2 + 5)$ is even for any $n\in \mathbb{N} $.
problems.solution: Note that if $n$ is even then $n(n^2 + 5)$ is also even. Let $n$ is odd and write $n = 2k+1$ for some $k\in \mathbb{N} $. Then \begin{align*} n^2 + 5 & = (2k+1)^2 + 5 \\ & = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 + 5 \\ & = 2(k^2 + 2k + 3), \end{align*} is even and hence $n(n^2 + 5)$ is also even.

problems.title: Calculus - Increasing and decreasing function on some intervals
problems.problem: Let the function $ f(x) = \frac{x}{3} + \frac{3}{x} + 3, x \neq 0 $ be strictly increasing in $(-\infty, \alpha_1) \cup (\alpha_2, \infty)$ and strictly decreasing in $(\alpha_3, \alpha_4) \cup (\alpha_4, \alpha_5)$. Then $ \sum\limits_{i=1}^{5} \alpha_i^2 $ is equal to \rule{1.9cm}{1pt}.
problems.solution:
The given function is \[ f(x) = \frac{x}{3} + \frac{3}{x} + 3, \ x \neq 0. \] Observe that \begin{align*} f'(x) = \frac{1}{3} - \frac{3}{x^2 }. \end{align*} Therefore, $f$ is strictly increasing if \begin{align*} f'(x) > 0 & \implies \frac{1}{3} - \frac{3}{x^2} >0 \\ & \implies \frac{x^2 - 9}{3x^2} > 0 \\ & \implies x^2 - 9 > 0 \\ & \implies (x-3)(x+3) > 0\\ & \implies x \in (-\infty ,-3) \cup (3, \infty ). \end{align*}
It is strictly decreasing if \begin{align*} f'(x) < 0 & \implies (x-3)(x+3) < 0\\ & \implies x\in (-3,3) \setminus \{ 0 \} \\ & \implies x \in (-3, 0) \cup (0,3). \end{align*} Therefore, $\alpha _1 = -3, \alpha _2 = 3, \alpha _3 = -3, \alpha _4 = 0$ and $\alpha _5 = 3$. Thus, \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{5} \alpha _i^2 = 4 \times 3^2 = 36. \end{align*}

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.3 - Set Theory - Describe the following sets verbally
problems.problem:
If $A$ is the set of all residents of the United States, $B$ the set of all Canadian citizens, and $C$ the set of all women in the world, then describe the sets
    \[
        A  \cap B  \cap C, \quad A - B, \quad A - C, \quad C - A
    \]
    verbally.
problems.solution:
The sets can be described verbally as follows:
  1. $A \cap B \cap C$ is the set of all women who are both residents of the United States and Canadian citizens.
  2. $A - B$ is the set of all residents of the United States who are not Canadian citizens.
  3. $A - C$ is the set of all residents of the United States who are not women.
  4. $C - A$ is the set of all women in the world who are not residents of the United States.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.4 - Set Theory - Find the value of a if the intersection of two sets is given
problems.problem: If $A = \{ 1,4,7,a \} $ and $B = \{ 3,4,9,11 \} $ and you have been told that $A  \cap B = \{ 4,9 \} $, what must $a$ be?
problems.solution: Note that $A \cap B = \{ 4,9 \}$. Since $4 \in A$ and $4 \in B$, it is clear that $4$ is in the intersection. However, $9$ is not in set $A$ as given. Therefore, for the intersection to contain $9$, we must have $a = 9$. Thus, the value of $a$ must be $9$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.6 - Set Theory - Prove that A union C is a subset of B union C if A is a subset of B
problems.problem: If $A \subset B$, prove that $A  \cup C \subset B  \cup C$ for any set $C$.
problems.solution:
Let $x \in A \cup C$. Then either $x \in A$ or $x \in C$.
  • If $x \in A$, then since $A \subset B$, we have $x \in B$. Therefore, $x \in B \cup C$.
  • If $x \in C$, then clearly $x \in B \cup C$.
In both cases, we have shown that $x \in B \cup C$. Therefore, $A \cup C \subset B \cup C$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.7 - Set Theory - Prove that A union B equals B union A and A intersection B equals B intersection A
problems.problem: Show that $A  \cup B = B  \cup A$ and $A \cap B = B \cap A$.
problems.solution:
Let $x \in A \cup B$. Then either $x \in A$ or $x \in B$.
  • If $x \in A$, then clearly $x \in B \cup A$.
  • If $x \in B$, then clearly $x \in B \cup A$.
In both cases, we have shown that $x \in B \cup A$. Therefore, $A \cup B \subset B \cup A$. By a similar argument, we can show that $B \cup A \subset A \cup B$. Thus, we conclude that $A \cup B = B \cup A$.
Now let $x \in A \cap B$. Then $x$ is in both $A$ and $B$. Since the intersection is commutative, it follows that $x$ is also in both $B$ and $A$. Therefore, $x \in B \cap A$, and we have shown that $A \cap B = B \cap A$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.8 - Set Theory - Prove that (A - B) union (B - A) equals (A union B) - (A intersection B)
problems.problem: Prove that $(A - B)  \cup (B - A) = (A  \cup B) - (A \cap B)$. What does this look pictorially?
problems.solution:
Let $x \in (A - B) \cup (B - A)$. Then either $x \in A - B$ or $x \in B - A$.
  • If $x \in A - B$, then $x \in A$ and $x \notin B$. Therefore, $x \in A \cup B$ and $x \notin A \cap B$, which implies that $x \in (A \cup B) - (A \cap B)$.
  • If $x \in B - A$, then $x \in B$ and $x \notin A$. Therefore, $x \in A \cup B$ and $x \notin A \cap B$, which implies that $x \in (A \cup B) - (A \cap B)$.
In both cases, we have shown that $x \in (A \cup B) - (A \cap B)$. Therefore, $(A - B) \cup (B - A) \subseteq (A \cup B) - (A \cap B)$.
Conversely, let $y \in (A \cup B) - (A \cap B)$. Then $y$ is in either $A$ or $B$, but not in both. If $y$ is in $A$ but not in $B$, then $y \in A - B$. If $y$ is in $B$ but not in $A$, then $y \in B - A$. In either case, we have shown that $y$ is in $(A - B) \cup (B - A)$. Therefore, $(A \cup B) - (A \cap B) = (A - B) \cup (B - A)$.
Pictorially, this represents the symmetric difference of sets $A$ and $B$, which consists of the elements that are in either set but not in their intersection.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.9 - Set Theory - Prove that A intersection (B union C) equals (A intersection B) union (A intersection C)
problems.problem:
Prove that 
    \[
        A  \cap (B  \cup C) = (A  \cap B)  \cup (A  \cap C).
    \]
problems.solution:
Let $x \in A \cap (B \cup C)$. Then $x \in A$ and $x \in B \cup C$. Since $x \in B \cup C$, it follows that either $x \in B$ or $x \in C$. If $x \in B$, then $x \in A \cap B$. If $x \in C$, then $x \in A \cap C$. In either case, we have shown that $x \in (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$. Therefore, $A \cap (B \cup C) \subseteq (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$.
Conversely, let $y \in (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$. Then either $y \in A \cap B$ or $y \in A \cap C$. If $y \in A \cap B$, then $y$ is in both $A$ and $B$, which implies that $y$ is in both $A$ and $B \cup C$. If $y \in A \cap C$, then $y$ is in both $A$ and $C$, which implies that $y$ is in both $A$ and $B \cup C$. In either case, we have shown that $y$ is in both sets. Therefore, $(A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C) = A \cap (B \cup C)$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.10 - Set Theory - Prove that A union (B intersection C) equals (A union B) intersection (A union C)
problems.problem:
Prove that 
    \[
        A  \cup (B  \cap C) = (A  \cup B)  \cap (A  \cup C).
    \]
problems.solution:
Let $x \in A \cup (B \cap C)$. Then \begin{align*} x \in A \text{ and } \in B \cap C & \implies x \in A \text{ or } x \in B \cap C \\ & \implies x \in A \text{ or } (x \in B \text{ and } x \in C) \\ & \implies (x \in A \text{ or } x \in B) \text{ and } (x \in A \text{ or } x \in C) \\ & \implies x \in (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C). \end{align*}
Conversely, let $y \in (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)$. Then \begin{align*} y \in (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C) & \implies y \in (A \cup B) \text{ and } y \in (A \cup C) \\ & \implies (y \in A \text{ or } y \in B) \text{ and } (y \in A \text{ or } y \in C) \\ & \implies y \in A \text{ or } (y \in B \text{ and } y \in C) \\ & \implies y \in A \cup (B \cap C). \end{align*}

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.11 - Set Theory - List all the subsets of a given set
problems.problem: Write down all the subsets of $S = \{ 1,2,3,4 \} $.
problems.solution:
We will list all the subsets of $S$ by looking at the number of elements in each subset.
  • The empty set: $\emptyset$.
  • Subsets with one element: $\{ 1 \}, \{ 2 \}, \{ 3 \}, \{ 4 \}$.
  • Subsets with two elements: $\{ 1,2 \}, \{ 1,3 \}, \{ 1,4 \}, \{ 2,3 \}, \{ 2,4 \}, \{ 3,4 \}$.
  • Subsets with three elements: $\{ 1,2,3 \}, \{ 1,2,4 \}, \{ 1,3,4 \}, \{ 2,3,4 \}$.
  • The subset with all four elements: $\{ 1,2,3,4 \}$.
Therefore, the total number of subsets of $S$ is $16$, and they are: \begin{align*} & \emptyset, \{ 1 \}, \{ 2 \}, \{ 3 \}, \{ 4 \}, \{ 1,2 \}, \{ 1,3 \}, \{ 1,4 \}, \{ 2,3 \}, \\ & \quad \{ 2,4 \}, \{ 3,4 \}, \{ 1,2,3 \}, \{ 1,2,4 \}, \{ 1,3,4 \}, \{ 2,3,4 \}, \{ 1,2,3,4\}. \end{align*}

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.12 - Set Theory - Prove the De Morgan Rules for subsets
problems.problem:
If $C$ is a subset of $S$, let $C'$ denote the complement of $C$ in $S$. Prove the De Morgan Rules for subsets $A,B$ of $S$, namely:
  1. $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$.
  2. $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$.
problems.solution:
1. Let $x \in (A \cap B)'$. Then $x otin A \cap B$, which means that $x$ is not in either $A$ or $B$. Therefore, either $x otin A$ or $x otin B$, which implies that $x \in A'$ or $x \in B'$. Thus, $x \in A' \cup B'$, and we have shown that $(A \cap B)' \subseteq A' \cup B'$. Conversely, let $y \in A' \cup B'$. Then either $y \in A'$ or $y \in B'$, which means that either $y otin A$ or $y otin B$. This implies that $y otin A \cap B$. Thus, $y \in (A \cap B)'$, and we have shown that $A' \cup B' \subseteq (A \cap B)'$. Combining both inclusions, we conclude that $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$.
  2. Let $x \in (A \cup B)'$. Then $x otin A \cup B$, which means that $x$ is not in $A$ and not in $B$. Therefore, $x otin A$ and $x otin B$, which implies that $x \in A'$ and $x \in B'$. Thus, $x \in A' \cap B'$, and we have shown that $(A \cup B)' \subseteq A' \cap B'$. Conversely, let $y \in A' \cap B'$. Then $y$ is in both complements, which means that $y$ is not in either set. Therefore, $y$ is not in the union of the two sets, which implies that $y otin A \cup B$. Thus, $y \in (A \cup B)'$, and we have shown that $A' \cap B' \subseteq (A \cup B)'$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.13 - Set Theory - Prove the following properties of the operations + and .
problems.problem:
Let $S$ be a set. For any two subsets of $S$ we define \[ A + B \coloneqq (A - B) \cup (B - A) \text{ and } A \cdot B \coloneqq A \cap B. \] Prove that
  1. $A + B = B + A$.
  2. $A + \varnothing = A$.
  3. $A \cdot A = A$.
  4. $A + A = \varnothing $.
  5. $A + (B + C) = (A + B) + C.$
  6. If $A + B = A + C,$ then $B = C$.
  7. $A \cdot (B + C) = A \cdot B + A \cdot C.$
problems.solution:
1. We have \begin{align*} A + B & = (A - B) \cup (B - A) \\ & = (B - A) \cup (A - B) \\ & = B + A. \end{align*}
  2. Note that \begin{align*} A + \varnothing & = (A - \varnothing ) \cup (\varnothing - A) \\ & = A \cup \varnothing \\ & = A. \end{align*}
  3. We have \begin{align*} A \cdot A & = A \cap A = A. \end{align*}
  4. We have \begin{align*} A + A & = (A - A) \cup (A - A) \\ & = \varnothing \cup \varnothing = \varnothing . \end{align*}
  5. Note that \begin{align*} A + (B + C) & = A + ((B - C) \cup (C - B)) \\ & = (A - ((B - C) \cup (C - B))) \\ & \quad \cup (((B - C) \cup (C - B)) - A) \\[1ex] & = ((A - (B - C)) \cap (A - (C - B))) \\ & \quad \cup (((B - C) \cup (C - B)) - A) \\[1ex] & = ((A - B) \cup (A - C)) \cup (((B - C) \cup (C - B)) - A) \\[1ex] & = ((A - B) \cup ((B - C) \cup (C - B))) \\ & \quad \cup ((A - C) \cup (((B - C) \cup (C - B)) - A)) \\[1ex] & = ((A + B) + C). \end{align*}
  6. We have \begin{align*} A \cdot (B + C) & = A \cdot \left( (B - C) \cup (C - B) \right) \\ & = A \cap \left( (B - C) \cup (C - B) \right) \\ & = \left[ A \cap (B - C) \right] \cup \left[ A \cap (C - B) \right] \\ & = \left[ (A \cap B) - (A \cap C) \right] \cup \left[ (A \cap C) - (A \cap B) \right] \\ & = (A \cdot B) + (A \cdot C). \end{align*}

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.14 - Set Theory - Prove the inclusion-exclusion principle for two finite sets
problems.problem:
If $C$ is a finite set, let $m(C)$ denote the number of elements in $C$. If $A, B$ are finite sets, prove that
    \[
        m(A  \cup B) = m(A) + m(B) - m(A  \cap B).
    \]
problems.hint: • $x \in A \cup B$ means $x \in A$ or $x \in B$. So the intersection is being counted twice.
problems.solution:
Note that $x \in A \cup B$ if and only if $x \in A$ or $x \in B$. However, if $x \in A \cap B$, then $x$ is counted twice in the sum $m(A) + m(B)$. Therefore, we must subtract $m(A \cap B)$ to avoid double counting.
Thus, we have \[ m(A \cup B) = m(A) + m(B) - m(A \cap B). \]

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.15 - Set Theory - Find a formula for the union of three finite sets
problems.problem: For three finite sets $A, B, C$ find a formula for $m(A  \cup B  \cup C).$
problems.hint: • First consider $D = B \cup C$ and use the formula for two sets. Then apply the formula for two sets again to $A$ and $D$.
problems.solution:
Recall that from the previous problem (1.2.14), we know that \begin{equation}\label{eq:20Sep2025-1} m(A \cup B) = m(A) + m(B) - m(A \cap B). \end{equation} Let $D = B \cup C$. Then, by the equation \eqref{eq:20Sep2025-1}, we have \[ m(D) = m(B) + m(C) - m(B \cap C). \] Applying the formula for two sets to $A$ and $D$, we get \[ m(A \cup B \cup C) = m(A \cup D) = m(A) + m(D) - m(A \cap D). \] Substituting the expression for $m(D)$, we have \begin{align*} m(A \cup B \cup C) & = m(A) + m(D) - m(A \cap D) \\ & = m(A) + \left[ m(B) + m(C) - m(B \cap C) \right] - m(A \cap (B \cup C) ) \\[1ex] & = m(A) + m(B) + m(C) - m(B \cap C) \\ & \qquad - m((A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)). \end{align*}
Now, applying the formula for two sets to $A \cap B$ and $A \cap C$, we have \begin{align*} m((A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)) & = m(A \cap B) + m(A \cap C) - m((A \cap B) \cap (A \cap C)) \\ & = m(A \cap B) + m(A \cap C) - m(A \cap B \cap C). \end{align*}
Substituting this back into the previous expression, we get \begin{align*} m(A \cup B \cup C) & = m(A) + m(B) + m(C) \\ & \quad - m(B \cap C) - \left[ m(A \cap B) + m(A \cap C) - m(A \cap B \cap C) \right] \\[1ex] & = m(A) + m(B) + m(C) \\ & \quad - m(A \cap B) - m(A \cap C) - m(B \cap C) \\ & \quad + m(A \cap B \cap C). \end{align*} Therefore, \begin{align*} m(A \cup B \cup C) & = m(A) + m(B) + m(C) \\ & \quad - m(A \cap B) - m(A \cap C) - m(B \cap C) \\ & \quad + m(A \cap B \cap C). \end{align*}

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.16 - Set Theory - Find a formula for the number of elements in the union of n finite sets
problems.problem: Find a formula for the number of elements $m(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \dots \cup A_n)$ for $n$ finite sets $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$.
problems.hint: • Count how many times a single element $x$ lying in exactly $k$ of the sets gets counted by the right-hand side, and show this count is always $1$.
problems.solution:
We claim that \begin{align*} m(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \dots \cup A_n) &= \sum_{i=1}^{n} m(A_i) - \sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} m(A_i \cap A_j) \\ & \quad + \sum_{1 \le i < j < l \le n} m(A_i \cap A_j \cap A_l) \\ & \quad - \dots + (-1)^{n+1} m(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap \dots \cap A_n). \end{align*} Equivalently, indexing the sum over nonempty subsets $S \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, \begin{equation}\label{eq:27Sep2025-1} m\left( \bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i \right) = \sum_{\emptyset \neq S \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}} (-1)^{|S|+1} \, m\left( \bigcap_{i \in S} A_i \right). \end{equation}
Proof. Let $x$ be an arbitrary element of $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \dots \cup A_n$. It suffices to show that $x$ is counted exactly once by the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:27Sep2025-1}; summing this fact over all $x \in A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_n$ then gives \eqref{eq:27Sep2025-1}, since elements outside the union contribute $0$ to both sides.
Since $x \in A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_n$, it belongs to at least one of the sets. Suppose $x$ belongs to exactly $k$ of the sets $A_1, \dots, A_n$, say \[ x \in A_{i_1}, A_{i_2}, \dots, A_{i_k}, \qquad x \notin A_j \text{ for all other } j, \] where $1 \le k \le n$.
For a nonempty subset $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$, the term $m\left(\bigcap_{i \in S} A_i\right)$ counts $x$ if and only if $x \in A_i$ for every $i \in S$, i.e., if and only if $S \subseteq \{i_1, \dots, i_k\}$. Thus the total contribution of $x$ to the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:27Sep2025-1} is \begin{align*} \sum_{\emptyset \neq S \subseteq \{i_1, \dots, i_k\}} (-1)^{|S|+1}. \end{align*} Grouping subsets by their size $r = |S|$, and noting there are $\binom{k}{r}$ subsets of $\{i_1, \dots, i_k\}$ of size $r$, this sum becomes \begin{align*} \sum_{\emptyset \neq S \subseteq \{i_1, \dots, i_k\}} (-1)^{|S|+1} &= \sum_{r=1}^{k} \binom{k}{r} (-1)^{r+1} \\ &= -\sum_{r=1}^{k} \binom{k}{r} (-1)^{r}. \end{align*} By the Binomial Theorem, \[ \sum_{r=0}^{k} \binom{k}{r} (-1)^r = (1-1)^k = 0, \] so that \[ \sum_{r=1}^{k} \binom{k}{r} (-1)^r = -\binom{k}{0} = -1. \] Substituting back, \[ \sum_{\emptyset \neq S \subseteq \{i_1, \dots, i_k\}} (-1)^{|S|+1} = -(-1) = 1. \]
Hence every element $x \in A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \dots \cup A_n$ is counted exactly once by the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:27Sep2025-1}, regardless of how many (at least one) of the sets $A_i$ it belongs to. Since elements not in the union contribute nothing to either side, the two sides of \eqref{eq:27Sep2025-1} are equal. This is exactly the inclusion-exclusion principle.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.17 - Set Theory - Show that at least 50% of Americans have both gone to high school and read a daily newspaper
problems.problem: Use the result of Problem 14 to show that if $80\%$ of all Americans have gone to high school and $70\%$ of all Americans read a daily newspaper then at least $50\%$ of Americans have both gone to high school and read a daily newspaper.
problems.hint: • Use the formula for two sets and the fact that $A \cup B$ is a subset of $U$, the set of all Americans.
problems.solution:
Let $A$ be the set of all Americans who have gone to high school and $B$ the set of all Americans who read a daily newspaper. Then we are given that \[ m(A) = 0.8m(U) \text{ and } m(B) = 0.7m(U), \] where $U$ is the set of all Americans. By the formula for two sets, we have \begin{align*} m(A \cup B) & = m(A) + m(B) - m(A \cap B) \\ & = 0.8m(U) + 0.7m(U) - m(A \cap B) \\ & = 1.5m(U) - m(A \cap B). \end{align*}
Since $A \cup B$ is a subset of $U$, we have $m(A \cup B) \le m(U)$, which implies that \begin{align*} 1.5m(U) - m(A \cap B) & \le m(U) \\ -m(A \cap B) & \le -0.5m(U) \\ m(A \cap B) & \ge 0.5m(U). \end{align*} Therefore, at least $50\%$ of Americans have both gone to high school and read a daily newspaper.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.18 - Set Theory - How many population agreed with the government on all three decisions
problems.problem: A public opinion poll shows that $93\%$ of the population agreed with the government on the first decision, $84\%$ on the second, and $74\%$ on the third, for three decisions made by the government.At least what percentage of the population agreed agreed with the government on all three decisions?
problems.hint:
• Note that for any subsets $X,Y$ of $U$, we have \[ m(X) + m(Y) - m(X \cap Y) \le m(U). \]
  • Use this to find a lower bound for $m(X \cap Y)$, and then apply it twice to the three sets of people who agreed with the government on each decision.
problems.solution:
Let $A, B, C$ be the sets of the population that agreed with the government on the first, second, and third decisions, respectively, and let $U$ be the set of all people in the population, so that \[ m(A) = 0.93\,m(U), \quad m(B) = 0.84\,m(U), \quad m(C) = 0.74\,m(U). \]
For any two subsets $X, Y$ of $U$, \[ m(X \cup Y) = m(X) + m(Y) - m(X \cap Y), \] and since $X \cup Y \subseteq U$, we have $m(X \cup Y) \le m(U)$. Hence \[ m(X) + m(Y) - m(X \cap Y) \le m(U), \] which rearranges to \begin{equation}\label{eq:11Oct2025-1} m(X \cap Y) \ge m(X) + m(Y) - m(U). \end{equation}
Applying \eqref{eq:11Oct2025-1} to $A$ and $B$, we have \begin{align*} m(A \cap B) & \ge m(A) + m(B) - m(U) \\ & = 0.93\,m(U) + 0.84\,m(U) - m(U) \\ & = 0.77\,m(U). \end{align*}
Now, applying \eqref{eq:11Oct2025-1} to $A \cap B$ and $C$, we have \begin{align*} m((A \cap B) \cap C) & \ge m(A \cap B) + m(C) - m(U) \\ & = 0.77\,m(U) + 0.74\,m(U) - m(U) \\ & = 0.51\,m(U). \end{align*} Therefore, at least $51\%$ of the population agreed with the government on all three decisions.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.19 - Set Theory - Solve Lewis Carroll's riddle about a group of disabled veterans
problems.problem:
In his book A Tangled Tale, Lewis Carroll proposed the following riddle about a group of disabled veterans:

Say that $70\%$ have lost an eye, $75\%$ an ear, $80\%$ an arm, $85\%$ a leg. What percentage at least, must have lost all four?

Solve Lewis Carroll's problem.
problems.hint:
• Note that for any subsets $X,Y$ of $U$, we have \[ m(X) + m(Y) - m(X \cap Y) \le m(U). \]
  • Use this to find a lower bound for $m(X \cap Y)$, and then apply it three times to the four sets of veterans who have lost an eye, an ear, an arm, and a leg.
problems.solution:
Let $A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4$ be the sets of veterans who have lost an eye, an ear, an arm, and a leg, respectively. Then we are given that \begin{align*} m(A_1) & = 0.70\,m(U), \\ m(A_2) & = 0.75\,m(U), \\ m(A_3) & = 0.80\,m(U), \\ m(A_4) & = 0.85\,m(U), \end{align*} where $U$ is the set of all veterans.
For any two subsets $X, Y$ of $U$, \[ m(X \cup Y) = m(X) + m(Y) - m(X \cap Y), \] and since $X \cup Y \subseteq U$, we have $m(X \cup Y) \le m(U)$. Hence \[ m(X) + m(Y) - m(X \cap Y) \le m(U), \] which rearranges to \begin{equation}\label{eq:18Oct2025-1} m(X \cap Y) \ge m(X) + m(Y) - m(U). \end{equation}
Applying \eqref{eq:18Oct2025-1} to $A_1$ and $A_2$, we have \begin{align*} m(A_1 \cap A_2) &\ge m(A_1) + m(A_2) - m(U) \\ & = 0.70\,m(U) + 0.75\,m(U) - m(U) \\ & = 0.45\,m(U). \end{align*}
Now, applying \eqref{eq:18Oct2025-1} to $A_1 \cap A_2$ and $A_3$, we have \begin{align*} m\big((A_1 \cap A_2) \cap A_3\big) \ge m(A_1 \cap A_2) + m(A_3) - m(U). \end{align*} Substituting the bound we get, \begin{align*} m(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3) & \ge m(A_1 \cap A_2) + m(A_3) - m(U) \\ & \ge 0.45\,m(U) + 0.80\,m(U) - m(U) \\ & = 0.25\,m(U). \end{align*}
Finally, applying \eqref{eq:18Oct2025-1} to $A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3$ and $A_4$, we have \begin{align*} m\big((A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3) \cap A_4\big) \ge m(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3) + m(A_4) - m(U). \end{align*} Substituting the bound we get, \begin{align*} m(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3 \cap A_4) & \ge m(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap A_3) + m(A_4) - m(U) \\ & \ge 0.25\,m(U) + 0.85\,m(U) - m(U) \\ & = 0.10\,m(U). \end{align*} Therefore, at least $10\%$ of the population must have lost all four body parts.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.20 - Set Theory - Show that for finite sets A, B, that m(A x B) = m(A) * m(B)
problems.problem: Show, for finite sets $A, B$, that $m(A \times B) = m(A) \cdot m(B)$.
problems.hint: • Note that for each element of $A$, there are $m(B)$ number of choices and hence in total $m(A) \cdot m(B)$.
problems.solution:
Let $A = \{ a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m \}$ and $B = \{ b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n \}$ be finite sets with $m(A) = m$ and $m(B) = n$. The Cartesian product $A \times B$ consists of all ordered pairs $(a_i, b_j)$ where $a_i \in A$ and $b_j \in B$.
For each element $a_i$ in $A$, there are exactly $n$ elements in $B$, resulting in $n$ ordered pairs of the form $(a_i, b_j)$ for each $j = 1, 2, \dots, n$. Since there are $m$ elements in $A$, the total number of ordered pairs in $A \times B$ is given by: \[ m(A \times B) = m \cdot n. \] Therefore, we conclude that: \[ m(A \times B) = m(A) \cdot m(B). \]

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.21 - Set Theory: Find the number of subsets of a set with 5 elements
problems.problem:
If $S$ is a set having five elements:
  1. How many subsets does $S$ have?
  2. How many subsets having four elements does $S$ have?
  3. How many subsets having two elements does $S$ have?
problems.hint: • The total number of subsets of a set with $n$ elements is $2^n$.
problems.solution:
Given that the set $S$ has five elements, we can denote it as $S = \{ s_1, s_2, s_3, s_4, s_5 \}$. Let us count all the subsets of $S$ by looking at the number of elements in each subset.
  • The empty set: $\emptyset$.
  • Subsets with one element: Since there are $5$ elements in the set, the number of subsets with one element is $5$.
  • Subsets with two elements: The number of ways to choose $2$ elements from $5$ is given by the binomial coefficient $\binom{5}{2} = 10$.
  • Subsets with three elements: The number of ways to choose $3$ elements from $5$ is given by the binomial coefficient $\binom{5}{3} = 10$.
  • Subsets with four elements: The number of ways to choose $4$ elements from $5$ is given by the binomial coefficient $\binom{5}{4} = 5$.
  • The subset with all five elements is the set $S$ itself: $\{ s_1, s_2, s_3, s_4, s_5 \}$.
  1. The total number of subsets of $S$ is the sum of the number of subsets with different numbers of elements: \[ 1 + 5 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 = 32. \] In general, a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets. It also follows from the above calculation (as it is binomial sum) that the total number of subsets of a set with $n$ elements is $2^n$. Therefore, the total number of subsets of $S$ is $2^5 = 32$.
  2. The number of subsets having four elements is $\binom{5}{4} = 5$.
  3. The number of subsets having two elements is $\binom{5}{2} = 10$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.2.22 - Set Theory: Show that a set having n elements has 2^n elements and find the number of subsets that have exactly m elements
problems.problem:
1. Show that a set having $n$ elements has $2^n$ elements.
  2. If $0 < m < n$, how many subsets are there that have exactly $m$ elements?
problems.hint: • Use the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{m}$ to count the number of ways to choose $m$ elements from a set with $n$ elements.
problems.solution:
1. Let $S$ be a set with $n$ elements. Each element of $S$ can either be included in a subset or not. Therefore, for each of the $n$ elements, there are $2$ choices (include or exclude). Hence, the total number of subsets is given by: \[ 2 \times 2 \times \dots \times 2 = 2^n. \] Thus, a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets.
    We can also see by looking at the subsets of $S$ with $k$ elements, where $k = 0,1,\dots, n$.
    • The number of subsets with $0$ elements is $1$ (the empty set).
    • The number of subsets with $1$ element is $n$ (each element of $S$ can form a subset).
    • The number of subsets with $2$ elements is $\binom{n}{2}$ (the number of ways to choose $2$ elements from $n$).
    • The number of subsets with $3$ elements is $\binom{n}{3}$ (the number of ways to choose $3$ elements from $n$).
    • $\dots$
    • The number of subsets with $n$ elements is $1$ (the set $S$ itself).
    Therefore, the total number of subsets of $S$ is given by the sum: \[ 1 + n + \binom{n}{2} + \binom{n}{3} + \dots + \binom{n}{n-1} + 1 = 2^n. \] The above sum can be proved using the binomial expansion of $(x + y)^n$ with $x = y = 1$. \[ (1 + 1)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} = 2^n. \]
  2. The number of subsets that have exactly $m$ elements is given by the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{m}$, which counts the number of ways to choose $m$ elements from a set of $n$ elements. Therefore, the number of subsets with exactly $m$ elements is: \[ \binom{n}{m} = \frac{n!}{m!(n-m)!}. \]

problems.title: Herstein 1.3.1 - Mappings: Determine if a mapping is clearly and unambiguously defined
problems.problem:
For the given sets $S, T$ determine if a mapping $f: S \rightarrow T$ is clearly and unambiguously defined; if not, say why not.
  1. $S=$ set of all women, $T=$ set of all men, $f(s)=$ husband of $s$.
  2. $S=$ set of positive integers, $T=S, f(s)=s-1$.
  3. $S=$ set of positive integers, $T=$ set of nonnegative integers, $f(s)= s-1$.
  4. $S=$ set of nonnegative integers, $T=S, f(s)=s-1$.
  5. $S=$ set of all integers, $T=S, f(s)=s-1$.
  6. $S=$ set of all real numbers, $T=S, f(s)=\sqrt{s}$.
  7. $S=$ set of all positive real numbers, $T=S, f(s)=\sqrt{s}$.
problems.solution:
1. The mapping is not defined because not all women have husbands, and some women may have more than one husband (in the case of polygamy). Therefore, $f(s)$ is not defined for all $s \in S$.
  2. The mapping is not defined because $f(1) = 0$, which is not a positive integer. Therefore, $f(s)$ is not defined for all $s \in S$.
  3. The mapping is clearly defined because for every positive integer $s$, $f(s) = s - 1$ is a nonnegative integer. Therefore, $f(s)$ is defined for all $s \in S$.
  4. The mapping is not defined because $f(0) = -1$, which is not a nonnegative integer. Therefore, $f(s)$ is not defined for all $s \in S$.
  5. The mapping is clearly defined because for every integer $s$, $f(s) = s - 1$ is also an integer. Therefore, $f(s)$ is defined for all $s \in S$.
  6. The mapping is not defined because the square root of a negative real number is not a real number. Therefore, $f(s)$ is not defined for all $s \in S$.
  7. The mapping is clearly defined because for every positive real number $s$, $f(s) = \sqrt{s}$ is also a positive real number. Therefore, $f(s)$ is defined for all $s \in S$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.3.2 - Mappings: Determine if a mapping is 1-1, onto, or both
problems.problem: In those parts of Problem 1.3.1 where $f$ does define a function, determine if 1-1, onto, or both.
problems.hint:
• A function $f: S \rightarrow T$ is 1-1 (injective) if for every $s_1, s_2 \in S$, $f(s_1) = f(s_2)$ implies $s_1 = s_2$.
  • A function $f: S \rightarrow T$ is onto (surjective) if for every $t \in T$, there exists an $s \in S$ such that $f(s) = t$.
problems.solution:
In the parts of Problem 1.3.1 where $f$ defines a function, we analyze each case for injectivity (1-1) and surjectivity (onto):
  1. Not applicable, as $f$ is not defined.
  2. Not applicable, as $f$ is not defined.
  3. The mapping $f(s) = s - 1$ from the set of positive integers to the set of nonnegative integers is both 1-1 and onto. It is 1-1 because if $f(s_1) = f(s_2)$, then $s_1 - 1 = s_2 - 1$, which implies $s_1 = s_2$. It is onto because for every nonnegative integer $t$, there exists a positive integer $s = t + 1$ such that $f(s) = t$.
  4. Not applicable, as $f$ is not defined.
  5. The mapping $f(s) = s - 1$ from the set of all integers to itself is both 1-1 and onto. It is 1-1 because if $f(s_1) = f(s_2)$, then $s_1 - 1 = s_2 - 1$, which implies $s_1 = s_2$. It is onto because for every integer $t$, there exists an integer $s = t + 1$ such that $f(s) = t$.
  6. Not applicable, as $f$ is not defined.
  7. The mapping $f(s) = \sqrt{s}$ from the set of all positive real numbers to itself is both 1-1 and onto. It is 1-1 because if $f(s_1) = f(s_2)$, then $\sqrt{s_1} = \sqrt{s_2}$, which implies $(\sqrt{s_1})^2 = (\sqrt{s_2})^2$, and thus $s_1 = s_2$. It is onto because for every positive real number $t$, there exists a positive real number $s = t^2$ such that $f(s) = t$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.3.3 - Mappings: Prove that the inverse of a 1-1 mapping is also a 1-1 mapping
problems.problem: If $f$ is a 1-1 mapping of $S$ onto $T$, prove that $f^{-1}$ is a 1-1 mapping of $T$ onto $S$.
problems.hint: • Since $f$ is a 1-1 mapping of $S$ onto $T$, for every $t \in T$, there exists a unique element $s \in S$ such that $f(s) = t$. Hence the inverse function $f^{-1}: T \to S$ is well-defined by $f^{-1}(t) = s \iff f(s) = t$.
problems.solution:
Since $f:S\to T$ is a one-to-one mapping of $S$ onto $T$, for every $t\in T$ there exists a unique element $s\in S$ such that \[ f(s)=t. \] Hence the inverse function $f^{-1}:T\to S$ is well-defined by \[ f^{-1}(t)=s \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad f(s)=t. \]
We first show that $f^{-1}$ is one-to-one. Let $t_1,t_2\in T$ and suppose \[ f^{-1}(t_1)=f^{-1}(t_2). \] Let this common value be $s\in S$. Then, by the definition of the inverse function, \[ f(s)=t_1 \quad \text{and} \quad f(s)=t_2. \] Therefore, \[ t_1=t_2. \] Hence $f^{-1}$ is one-to-one.
Next, we show that $f^{-1}$ is onto. Let $s\in S$. Since $f$ is a mapping from $S$ to $T$, we have $f(s)\in T$. Put \[ t=f(s). \] Then, by the definition of the inverse function, \[ f^{-1}(t)=s. \] Thus, for every $s\in S$, there exists a $t\in T$ such that \[ f^{-1}(t)=s. \] Hence $f^{-1}$ is onto. Therefore, $f^{-1}$ is a one-to-one mapping of $T$ onto $S$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.3.4 - Mappings: Prove that the composition of a mapping and its inverse is the identity mapping
problems.problem: If $f$ is a 1-1 mapping of $S$ onto $T$, prove that $f^{-1} \circ f = i_S$, where $i_S$ is the identity mapping of $S$ onto itself.
problems.hint: • Since $f$ is a 1-1 mapping of $S$ onto $T$, for every $s \in S$, there exists a unique $t \in T$ such that $f(s) = t$. Hence the inverse function $f^{-1}: T \to S$ is well-defined by $f^{-1}(t) = s \iff f(s) = t$.
problems.solution: We need to prove that for every $s \in S$, we have $(f^{-1} \circ f)(s) = i_S(s) = s$. By the definition of the composition of functions, we have \[ (f^{-1} \circ f)(s) = f^{-1}(f(s)). \] Since $f$ is a 1-1 mapping of $S$ onto $T$, for every $s \in S$, there exists a unique $t \in T$ such that $f(s) = t$. By the definition of the inverse function, we have \[ f^{-1}(t) = s \quad \text{if and only if} \quad f(s) = t. \] Therefore, substituting $t = f(s)$, we get \[ f^{-1}(f(s)) = s. \] Hence, for every $s \in S$, we have \[ (f^{-1} \circ f)(s) = s = i_S(s). \] Therefore, we conclude that \[ f^{-1} \circ f = i_S. \]

problems.title: Herstein 1.3.5 - Mappings: Prove that the composition of two onto mappings is also onto
problems.problem:
Give a proof of the Remark after Lemma 1.3.2. The remark is

Remark

If $g: S \to T$ and $f: T \to U$ are both onto, then $f \circ g: S \to U$ is also onto.
problems.hint: • Use $f$ being onto to get en element in $T$ and then use $g$ is onto to get a preimage in $S$.
problems.solution: Given that $g: S \to T$ and $f: T \to U$ are both onto, we need to show that the composition $f \circ g: S \to U$ is also onto. Let $u \in U$ be given. Since $f: T \to U$ is onto, there exists $t \in T$ such that $f(t) = u$. For this $t \in T$, since $g: S \to T$ is onto, there exists $s \in S$ such that $g(s) = t$. Therefore, we have \[ (f \circ g)(s) = f(g(s)) = f(t) = u. \] Since $u \in U$ was arbitrary, we conclude that for every $u \in U$, there exists $s \in S$ such that $(f \circ g)(s) = u$. Hence, $f \circ g: S \to U$ is onto.

problems.title: Herstein 1.3.6 - Mappings: Prove that if f is onto and g∘f = h∘f, then g = h
problems.problem: If $f: S \to  T$ is onto and $g: T \to  U$ and $h: T \to  U$ are such that $g\circ f = h\circ f$, prove that $g = h$.
problems.hint: • Use the fact that $f$ is onto to find a preimage in $S$ for an arbitrary element in $T$. Then use the equality $g \circ f = h \circ f$ to show that $g(t) = h(t)$ for all $t \in T$.
problems.solution: Let $t \in T$ be arbitrary. Since $f$ is onto, there exists $s \in S$ such that $f(s) = t$. Then we have \begin{align*} g(t) = g(f(s)) = (g \circ f)(s) = (h \circ f)(s) = h(f(s)) = h(t). \end{align*} Since $t \in T$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $g(t) = h(t)$ for all $t \in T$. Therefore, $g = h$.

problems.title: Herstein 1.3.7 - Mappings: Prove that if f is 1-1 and f∘g = f∘h, then g = h
problems.problem: If $g: S \to T, \, h: S \to  T$ and if $f: T \to U$ is 1-1, show that if $f\circ g = f\circ h$, then $g = h$.
problems.hint: • Use the fact that $f$ is 1-1 to show that $g(s) = h(s)$ for all $s \in S$.
problems.solution: Let $s \in S$ be arbitrary. Then we have \[ (f \circ g)(s) = (f \circ h)(s). \] By the definition of composition, this means \[ f(g(s)) = f(h(s)). \] Since $f$ is 1-1, we can conclude that \[ g(s) = h(s). \] Since $s \in S$ was arbitrary, we conclude that $g(s) = h(s)$ for all $s \in S$. Therefore, $g = h$.

problems.title: Number Theory - n^7 - n is divisible by 42
problems.problem: Show that $n^7 - n$ is divisible by $42$ for every positive integer $n$.
problems.hint:
• A number is divisible by $42$ if it is divisible by $6$ and $7$.
  • Use Fermat's Little Theorem to show that it is divisible by $7$.
problems.solution:
Note that a number is divisible by $42$ if it is divisible by $7$ and $6$, that is, divisible by $7,2$ and $3$. Now we have \begin{align*} n^7 - n & = n(n^6 - 1) = n ((n^2)^3 - 1) \\ & = n (n^2 - 1)(n^4 + n^2 + 1) \\ & = n (n-1)(n+1) (n^4 + n^2 + 1). \end{align*} Since the product any three consecutive integers is divisible by $6$, so $n^7 - n$ is divisible by $6$.
To show that it is divisible by $7$, we will use Fermat's Little Theorem. By Fermat's Little Theorem, \[ n^7 \equiv n \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 7) \implies 7 \mid (n^7 - n). \] Therefore, the number $n^7 - n$ is divisible by $42$.

problems.title: Probability - The function fx) = 6x (1 - x) is a probability density function
problems.problem:
The diameter of an electric cable, say $X$ is assumed to be a continuous random variable with probability density function (pdf)
    \[
        f(x) = 6x (1 - x), \quad 0 \leq x\leq 1.
    \]
    Check that above is a pdf and determine a number $b$ such that $P(X < b) = P(X > b)$.
problems.hint:
• $f$ is pdf if $\int_{-\infty }^{\infty } f(x) \mathrm{d} x = 1$.
  • $P(X< b) = \int_0^b f(x) \mathrm{d} x$ and $P(x > b) = \int_b^1 f(x) \mathrm{d} x$.
problems.solution:
To see if the given function is a pdf or not, we will check if the total probability is $1$. That is, \begin{align*} \int_{-\infty }^ \infty f(x) \mathrm{d} x = 1. \end{align*} Note that, \begin{align*} \int_{-\infty }^ \infty f(x) \mathrm{d} x & \int_0^1 f(x) \mathrm{d} x \\ & = 6\int_0^1 x(1-x) \mathrm{d} x \\ & = 6 \int _0^1 (x - x^2) \mathrm{d} x \\ & = 6 \left[ \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_0^1 \\ & = 1. \end{align*}
Given that $P(X < b) = P(X > b)$, we have \begin{align*} & \int_0^b f(x) \mathrm{d} x = \int_b^1 f(x) \mathrm{d} x \\ \implies & 6 \int_0^b (x(1-x)) = 6 \int_1^b (x(1-x)) \\ \implies & \left[ \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_0^b = \left[ \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3} \right]_b^1 \\ \implies & \left( \frac{b^2}{2} - \frac{b^3}{3} \right) = \left[ \left( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3} \right) - \left( \frac{b^2}{2} - \frac{b^3}{3} \right) \right] \\ \implies & 3b^2 - 2b^3 = 1 - 3b^2 + 2b^3 \\ \implies & 4b^3 - 6b^2 + 1 = 0 \\ \implies & (2b -1)(2b^2 - 2b - 1) = 0 \\ \implies & 2b - 1 = 0, \quad \text{ since } 2b^2 - 2b - 1 >0. \end{align*} Thus $b = \frac{1}{2}$.

problems.title: NBHM - Find the value of a in x^3 - 5x^2 + ax - 1
problems.problem:
Find the value of $a \in \mathbb{Z} $ such that $2 + \sqrt{3} $ is a root of the polynomial 
    \[
        p(x) = x^3 - 5x^2 + ax - 1.
    \]
problems.hint:
• The irrational roots are in conjugate pairs.
  • Apply ratioanl root theorem.
problems.solution: By ratioanl root theorem, the only possible rational roots are $\pm 1$. Also, since the polynomial is with integer coefficients, any irrational root will be in pair (with its conjugate). Therefore the possible roots are \[ \{ 2 + \sqrt{3} , 2 - \sqrt{3} , 1 \} \quad \text{ or } \{ 2 + \sqrt{3} , 2 - \sqrt{3} , -1 \}. \] Recall that the sum of roots of a polynomial \[ a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1 x + a_0, \] is $-\frac{a_{n-1} }{a_n}$. So in our case it is $5$. Therefore the roots are $\{ 2 + \sqrt{3} , 2 - \sqrt{3} , 1 \}.$ Therefore, \begin{align*} a & = (2 + \sqrt{3} ) (2 - \sqrt{3} ) + (2 + \sqrt{3} )(1) + (2-\sqrt{3} )(1) \\ & = (4 -3) + 2 + \sqrt{3} + 2 - \sqrt{3} \\ & = 5. \end{align*} Thus, $a = 5$.

problems.title: Calculus - NBHM - 2005 - div(curl(v)) = 0
problems.problem:
Let $\mathbf{v} = (v_1, v_2. v_3)$ be a vector field on $\mathbb{R} ^3$ where
    \[
        v_1 = \sqrt{1 + x^2 + y^2} , v_2 = \sqrt{1+ z^2} \text{ and } v_3 = \sqrt{1+ x^2 y^2 z^2}.
    \]
    Evaluate $\mathrm{div} (\mathrm{curl}(\mathbf{v} ) )$.
problems.hint: • Recall that if the components of a vector field have continuous second-order partial derivatives, then $\mathrm{div}(\mathrm{curl}(\mathbf{v})) = 0$.
problems.solution:
The curl of a vector field $\mathbf{v} = (v_1,v_2,v_3)$ is given by \[ \nabla \times \mathbf{v} = \left( \frac{\partial v_3}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial v_2}{\partial z}, \frac{\partial v_1}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial v_3}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial v_2}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial v_1}{\partial y} \right). \]
Taking the divergence, we obtain \begin{align*} \nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \frac{\partial v_3}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial v_2}{\partial z} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( \frac{\partial v_1}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial v_3}{\partial x} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \left( \frac{\partial v_2}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial v_1}{\partial y} \right) \\[0.5em] &= \frac{\partial^2 v_3}{\partial x \partial y} - \frac{\partial^2 v_2}{\partial x \partial z} + \frac{\partial^2 v_1}{\partial y \partial z} - \frac{\partial^2 v_3}{\partial y \partial x} + \frac{\partial^2 v_2}{\partial z \partial x} - \frac{\partial^2 v_1}{\partial z \partial y}. \end{align*} Since the functions $v_1, v_2,$ and $v_3$ have continuous second-order partial derivatives on $\mathbb{R}^3$, the mixed partial derivatives commute: \[ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x}. \] Hence, each pair of terms cancels, and we conclude that \[ \nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) = 0. \] Therefore, \[ \boxed{\mathrm{div}(\mathrm{curl}(\mathbf{v})) = 0.} \]

problems.title: NBHM 2005 - Find the area of the triangle
problems.problem: What is the area of the triangle in the complex plane formed by the points representing $1, \omega $ and $\omega ^2$, where $\omega $ is a complex cube root of unity?
problems.hint: • Draw picture and note that it is an equilateral triangle.
problems.solution:
We need to find the area of the triangle formed by the points representing $1, \omega $ and $\omega ^2$. The triangle is equilateral triangle and the side length is \begin{align*} \left\vert 1 - \omega \right\vert^2 = \left\vert \left( \frac{3}{2} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{-\sqrt{3} }{2} \right)^2 \right\vert = 3. \end{align*}
